The Old Photo
Many years before our shlichus, the
Rebbe’s bracha had already begun.
“You won’t believe what I just heard,”Tatty
told Mommy one day. “There’s a big, beautiful
property for sale right here in Olympia!”
They could already imagine it: shiurim,
farbrengens, and children’s programs, with
Yidden coming and going. A real home for our
Chabad House.
Tatty and Mommy raised money for the
down payment, but getting a bank loan
was harder.The bank needed a guarantor—
someone who would promise to pay if
Tatty couldn’t.
As the closing deadline came closer,Tatty
wrote to the Rebbe for a bracha.Then he met
with supporters to see if they could help.
But when the meeting ended, he still had
no guarantor.
How would they get the bank loan?
Right then, his phone pinged. It was a
message from Dr. K.
Dr. and Mrs. K. live far away in California, but
they support our Chabad House because
their daughter lives here.
Tatty opened the
message. “Amazing
news!” he exclaimed.
“Dr. K. agreed to be
the guarantor!”
Baruch Hashem, we
bought the property.
But we lived an hour’s
walk away, so we would
need to move closer.
Then, a few days later, the house near the
property went up for sale!
The Rebbe encouraged shluchim to buy
homes to show that they’re there to stay,
soTatty and Mommy decided to buy it.
They raised money, and once again, Dr. and
Mrs. K. helped.
Our shlichus was growing, but so were our
expenses. It was hard forTatty and Mommy
to cover the bills.
One day,Tatty got a message from Dr. K.
We’re coming to visit our daughter. Can we have
a meeting?
Uh oh. Tatty’s heart began to pound.Were

Chabad House?

my own.”

Dr. K. began: “My wife and I got married about
fifty years ago. For a long time, we waited
and waited for children.We went to the best
doctors, but nothing helped.Then, soon
after moving to Zaire, Africa, my wife became
pregnant with our daughter—the one who
lives here now! Later, we were also blessed
with a son.
“For years, we wondered how that miracle
happened. And now we know!”
Tatty held his breath. “What changed?”
“Recently, the Chabad rabbi where I live
showed me an old photo from Zaire in תשד”מ
(1984),” Dr. K. said. “It was found in a collection
of pictures sent to the Rebbe years ago.
My wife was in the photo! On the back, it
said that she lit Shabbos candles and kept
some mitzvos.
“But the most surprising thing was the date.
The photo was taken one month before
my wife became pregnant! I immediately
understood that the Rebbe had seen the
picture and blessed us with children.”
Tatty sat still in his seat, too amazed to speak.
“Who knows,” Dr. K. added with a smile.
“Maybe the Rebbe blessed us with a daughter
so that one day she would live in Olympia,
and we’d be able to help your Chabad House!
Well, let me tell you: I’ll continue my support
for as long as I can!”
Baruch Hashem, Dr. K. kept his word and
continued to support our Chabad House. And
the brachos didn’t stop there. Soon afterward,
Tatty saw more help with the finances, and
paying the bills became much easier.
He had been so worried about our financial
situation, and the Rebbe sent a clear message:
Long before our family moved on shlichus, the
Rebbe’s brachos had already begun.

Orders from our General
It’s easy to imagine someone who’s not free—a slave,
a prisoner, or a person who’s controlled by someone/
something else.
But what does it look like for someone to be free?
In this week’s parsha, Hashem tells Moshe Rabbeinu
that when theYidden leave Mitzrayim, they will come
to Har Sinai to serve Him. This shows the real reason
why the Yidden were freed: not just to stop being slaves
to Paroh, but to receive theTorah and serve Hashem.
When we Yidden serve Hashem, that is when we are
truly free.
There’s a hint to this in the way the Luchos were made.
The Aseres Hadibros were not written with ink or paint.
They were engraved into the actual stone.The Hebrew
word for engraving, “רּות ָ
ָח,” is very similar to the word
“ירּות ֵ
ֵח,” which means freedom.
By accepting the Luchos, which stand for the whole
Torah, theYidden became free—for real.

Malka Bracha’s group got on,
and soon enough, they were at
their usual mivtzoim spot—a
bike path near Prospect Park.
The girls stood near the path
with Shabbos candles in their
hands. “Excuse me, are you
Jewish?” they asked women
and girls who passed by.
But it wasn’t easy.
Bikers zoomed by. Joggers
hurried past. Everyone seemed
to be in a rush. The girls had
just a few seconds to get their
attention before they were
already gone.
Soon, a little girl came riding by
on her scooter with her nanny
walking beside her. Instead of
rushing past, she came over to
say hello.
“Is she Jewish?” the girls asked
the nanny.
“Yes, she is,” the nanny said
with a smile. “Her name is Noa.”
“I’m four!” Noa added proudly,
happy to meet new friends.
The girls gave Noa a special
princess-themed package of
Shabbos candles.
The nanny smiled. “Her
mother already lights.”
“These are for Noa,”
the girls explained.
“She can light Shabbos
candles, too!”
Noa’s face lit up. Her very
own Shabbos candles!
And they were princess-
themed; her favorite!
Bnos Menachem’s fourth graders headed to the
subway station with a bounce in their steps. It was
Friday, and that meant one thing: mivtzoim!
Each group was going to a different location with
its own madrichos. Our sister Malka Bracha was a
madricha for Group 5.
At the station, they made a rally and said pesukim.
Soon, the familiar screech of the subway filled the air.
Their train sped down the tracks, slowed to a stop, and
opened its doors.
